subject: history
title: Hopkins, the Civil War and Salem 1692
welcome_lead: Two iconic episodes: English Witchfinder General and the New England panic.
meta_desc: OCR A-Level adventure on Matthew Hopkins 1645-47 and the Salem witch trials of 1692.
final_note: You can compare the social mechanics of two famous witch panics.

concepts.def: Essex 'Witchfinder General' active 1645-47, responsible for c.100 of the c.300 English executions for witchcraft.
Anomalous bodily mark seen as evidence of demonic suckling; sought through 'pricking' and 'watching'.
Hopkins's first major investigation in Essex; resulted in around 19 executions at Chelmsford in July 1645.
Massachusetts outbreak: about 200 accused, 19 hanged, one pressed to death (Giles Corey), four died in jail.
Testimony that the accused's spirit had appeared to torment victims; admitted at Salem and later discredited.
Special tribunal convened by Governor Phips in May 1692 to try the Salem accused; dissolved October 1692.

walkthroughs.body_html: The First Civil War weakened normal judicial oversight in eastern England. Hopkins and John Stearne offered 'discovery' services for cash. Methods included sleep deprivation, walking and water-testing. The Manningtree investigation led to about 19 executions at Chelmsford (July 1645). John Gaule's Select Cases of Conscience (1646) criticised methods; Hopkins published The Discovery of Witches (1647). He died of tuberculosis in August 1647.

In January 1692, Salem Village girls including Abigail Williams and Betty Parris exhibited fits; Tituba was among the first accused. By summer, accusations spread up the social scale (Rebecca Nurse, Martha Corey). The Court of Oyer and Terminer began trials in June. Bridget Bishop was executed on 10 June. Nineteen were hanged on Gallows Hill; Giles Corey was pressed to death on 19 September.

Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience (October 1692) rejected spectral evidence. Phips dissolved the court; the Superior Court convicted only 3 of 56 in January 1693. Phips reprieved them. In 1697 Samuel Sewall publicly repented; in 1711 the colony reversed 22 convictions and compensated families. Salem became a byword for judicial folly.
